title: 2022 Forum Review | Kmart, Australia’s Largest National Brand, Embarks on a 3D Exploration Journey
description: Kmart is Australia's largest national department store brand. Operating over 326 stores in Australia and New Zealand, they have continuously explored new technologies in recent years and collaborated with CLO for digital transformation, comprehensively enhancing the brand's overall competitiveness. CLO specially invited Emerald, the senior 3D project leader from Kmart's China office, to share Kmart's experiences and insights in the process of digital transformation.
transcript:
Hello everyone, thanks for participating in the CLO Virtual User Summit.  
I am Ying, Business Director at the CLO Shanghai office.  
I'm so glad to have one of our CLO clients with us today, Ms. Emerald.  
She joined Kmart in October 2020 as a 3D manager, leading the 3D team and working on Project SQUARE to drive end-to-end digital transformation.  
Thank you for joining us, and we cannot wait to see your presentation.  
Okay, let's start.  

It's a pleasure to be here sharing some stories about our 3D journey.  
So, first of all, let me introduce our brand.  
Kmart Australia was established in 1969 and operates more than 326 stores throughout Australia and New Zealand.  
Let's see where our 3D projects come from.  
Our 3D exploration is a bit special.  
Instead of starting from a functional team, we launched a specialized project squad to drive our digital transformation.  
Currently, we have 10 team members.  
The squad is based in three regions, originating from six key functions in the apparel industry.  
This project started from scratch in October 2020.  
We made the software decision at the end of June last year after a series of trials and considerations from different aspects.  
Since then, we have completed two seasons of end-to-end development with the pilot department.  
We have seen great benefits from 3D,  
and the whole company is becoming more and more excited about this new way of working.  
All this success is thanks to the efforts and passion of the whole team and input from our stakeholders.  

Here, I would like to share something I recently heard from the Chinese media.  
There are so many answers in the world waiting for good questions.  
I find this especially relevant when we talk about 3D exploration.  
The most important thing is that the world is full of the unknown.  
In the industry, there are already many good resources.  
We have great concepts,  
amazing technologies, and talented users.  
All of these will support our digital revolution.  
But on the other hand, at least at the start, we face different choices.  
All these choices form different paths for the future.  
It will make a difference if we all start with good questions.  

Here, I would like to share some important questions and choices we have made.  
These represent where we are and who we are.  

So the first question is: which products shall we start with?  
Easy starts or difficult starts?  
We have to be realistic because we can't start everything at once, right?  
We’d better begin with a small group,  
create a small success, and then scale up once we have more certainty.  
If not speaking from an artist’s perspective, but from a commercial one,  
of course, life will be less tough if we start with easy styles—  
such as T-shirts or shirts, which have simple construction, consistent body shapes, and fabrics,  
and also have larger production volumes, which can demonstrate benefits most clearly.  
But after overall consideration, we made a bold decision to do the opposite:  
to start with difficult styles.  
We aimed to expose more issues at an early stage,  
so that we can be better prepared,  
and learn from failures when we can afford to.  
In this way, we can be more ready before scaling up to a larger scope.  

When we define difficult styles,  
we consider variation from both styling and fabric.  
The more variable the fabric is,  
the more handling considerations there are for both draping and appearance.  
And the more diverse the styling is,  
the more complex the construction to start in the digital world.  
These two factors actually multiply the difficulties.  
After reviewing all our categories,  
we finally chose to start with women's fashion.  
I just want to say,  
we have worked with many different styles,  
as it represents the most complex case for both.  
It almost overwhelmed us at the beginning.  
We had to satisfy the most demanding eyes of the development team,  
and we had to bear a heavier workload at the start.  
We had to overcome challenges from different styling features day by day,  
and also train 3D users in both software handling skills,  
as well as pattern and garment construction knowledge.  

Also,  
we needed good fabric resources.  
The resources for fabric digitization—I feel so proud of the team that we finally made it,  
and thanks to CLO for supporting all of this.  
Also,  
mastering this without backing from management would not have been possible.  
Taking this decision, working with so many challenges, and constantly pushing and breaking boundaries,  
our progress over the past six months has been remarkable.  

Since we made the 3D decision last season,  
our first sample approval rate in this department broke the record by 7%,  
and we have also achieved significant lead time reduction.  
These are the most challenging products. With easier products, there will be more room to win,  
and since we have these tricky products under control, there will be fewer product types to worry about in the future.  

The second question here is:  
what is our intention for the 3D operating model? In other words, how do we plan to use 3D?  
Shall we just use 3D simulation in prototyping, or are we prepared for digital transformation,  
changing the rules of the development game?  

Our choice is the latter. We want to change the way of working  
based on trust in 3D, instead of making it disconnected from development with physical samples.  
This means we have to  
make prototyping happen in the 3D world, and be able to do fitting and thorough reviews virtually.  

To support this decision, the first step is to make 3D realistic. We must gain confidence  
from stakeholders in 3D so that they are happy to replace most physical samples in development.  

Starting with fabric, we need to use the correct quality for digitization, and validate fabrics to  
achieve the desired accuracy before using them in 3D samples.  

Consistent avatars are also important. We need to have a twin set avatar in 3D.  

Correct 3D patterns are also crucial. Patterns used for 3D and patterns used for physical sampling  
will differ slightly. Also, when exporting patterns from 3D for physical sampling,  
different users might work in different ways.  

We must ensure the input and output patterns of 3D speak the same language  
by setting up standard 3D pattern criteria and building a tracking process.  

We have also gradually realized how important it is  
to apply suitable constructions to the 3D sample.  

Last but not least, other 3D-related knowledge needs to be refreshed through learning and correlation.  

We must agree that, at the current stage, 3D can't replace all physical samples. It can replace some,  
but not all. Correlation can give us more insights on handling improvements,  
fabric accuracy, and identify technical limitations, if any.  

With these learnings, the asset library and handling standards can be adjusted accordingly.  

Also, based on that, we can set realistic expectations for 3D samples,  
instead of getting lost in all these technical issues.  

The third question is: what is the ambition of our 3D journey?  
Technology-focused or the whole game?  

Further reflecting on the previous question, there is no doubt we choose to play  
the whole game. We need to roll out digital transformation in different aspects with different  
parties in order  
to win the whole game.  

Good 3D users are fundamental. User skills will decide how far we can go.  
We need to find the desired skill set for 3D users in different scenarios,  
then get better visibility of the skill map of in-house teams and suppliers,  
and make a proper upscaling plan.  

We also need to consider role evolution.  
There are already different roles in the traditional way of working, and there might be some  
new roles generated in the industry with a specialized focus.  

There is a funny story: I posted a role for a 3D merchandiser, and it took us five months to find a  
suitable person because many people had no idea what it was, and they still doubted if it  
was a real role.  

Also, the 3D prototyping process is important. When we invite people to join  
the new game, we must set up a clear agenda.  
We have to make sure that we have clear and realistic roles, so that everybody is happy to play.  

How do we ensure a more streamlined development life cycle? We rely on system integration.  

We still have a lot to do based on all these considerations, and all of us are confident  
and excited about a bigger, brighter future.  

The last question to share today is: how do we move forward? Faster alone or further together?  

Well, I think we can make decisions and move faster within a smaller group, but it might be  
risky if we just follow our own opinions in the industry journey, which might end up with some  
buy-offs. So we definitely choose to go further together, embracing small collaborations.  

In-house team members, suppliers, software companies, and other partners in the industry all  
play key roles in this new world.  

It's necessary to be open-minded, and it’s worth sharing resources and information with each  
other. Then we can get input and feedback to adjust the direction in line with  
industry trends. None of us can be quite sure about the future, but by working together,  
we can definitely create more possibilities.  

I really feel these forums are quite meaningful,  
which are great platforms to share information with each other.  

Thank you again for inviting me.  
I'm looking forward to a brighter future in the digital world with all of you.  
Thanks.

chunks.content: # 2022 Forum Review | Kmart, Australia’s Largest National Brand, Embarks on a 3D Exploration Journey This document presents a detailed overview of Kmart Australia's 3D exploration journey led by their 3D team, focusing on digital transformation in apparel development. It covers strategic decisions, technical approaches, challenges faced, and future ambitions related to 3D prototyping, digital workflows, and collaboration within the fashion industry. --- ## Introduction to Kmart Australia’s 3D Transformation Journey This section introduces Kmart Australia’s background, the origins of their 3D project squad, and the initial stages of their digital transformation using 3D technology. Kmart Australia, established in 1969, operates over 326 stores across Australia and New Zealand. In October 2020, Kmart formed a specialized 3D project squad consisting of 10 members from six key apparel industry functions, distributed across three regions. This squad was launched to spearhead an end-to-end digital transformation rather than evolving from a functional team. After extensive trials and considerations, the team finalized their 3D software choice in June 2021. Since then, they completed two full seasons of development with a pilot department, witnessing significant benefits and growing company-wide enthusiasm for their new digital workflows. The success was attributed to the team’s passion and stakeholder collaboration. --- ## Strategic Questions Guiding the 3D Exploration This section discusses key strategic questions Kmart addressed to shape their 3D journey, including product selection, operating model intentions, ambition level, and collaboration approach. ### 1. Which Products to Start With? Difficult or Easy Styles? Kmart faced a choice between starting with simple, easy-to-digitize products (e.g., T-shirts with simple construction and consistent fabrics) or more complex, difficult styles. Although easier styles would have reduced initial challenges and demonstrated benefits quickly, Kmart boldly chose to start with complex women’s fashion items. Difficult styles were defined by high variation in both styling and fabric, increasing complexity in digital draping, appearance, and garment construction. This decision aimed to expose more issues early, enabling better preparation and learning from failures when risks were manageable. Starting with complex styles required overcoming substantial challenges, including: - Meeting stringent expectations of the development team. - Managing heavier workloads. - Training 3D users in software handling and garment construction knowledge. - Securing high-quality fabric resources for accurate digitization, supported by CLO software and strong management backing. This approach yielded remarkable progress within six months. Since adopting 3D, the pilot department’s first sample approval rate improved by 7%, with significant lead time reductions. Mastering difficult products early provides a solid foundation for scaling to easier product categories. --- ## 3D Operating Model: Prototyping or Full Digital Transformation? This section outlines Kmart’s decision to fully integrate 3D into their development lifecycle, shifting from physical samples to virtual prototyping and reviews. Kmart chose to pursue a full digital transformation rather than using 3D solely for simulation during prototyping. The goal is to establish trust in 3D so stakeholders feel confident replacing most physical samples with virtual equivalents.

chunks.title: 2022 Forum Review | Kmart, Australia’s Largest National Brand, Embarks on a 3D Exploration Journey
chunks.content: Mastering difficult products early provides a solid foundation for scaling to easier product categories. --- ## 3D Operating Model: Prototyping or Full Digital Transformation? This section outlines Kmart’s decision to fully integrate 3D into their development lifecycle, shifting from physical samples to virtual prototyping and reviews. Kmart chose to pursue a full digital transformation rather than using 3D solely for simulation during prototyping. The goal is to establish trust in 3D so stakeholders feel confident replacing most physical samples with virtual equivalents. Key components of this model include: - **Realistic 3D Fabric Digitization:** Using high-quality fabrics and validating digitized materials to ensure accuracy in appearance and draping. - **Consistent Avatars:** Developing twin-set avatars in 3D to represent physical body shapes consistently. - **Standardized 3D Patterns:** Recognizing subtle differences between 3D and physical sampling patterns, Kmart established standard 3D pattern criteria and tracking processes to synchronize inputs and outputs. - **Appropriate Garment Construction:** Applying suitable construction techniques in 3D samples to mimic real-world garments. - **Continuous Learning and Knowledge Refreshing:** Updating skills and correlating 3D outputs with physical results to understand limitations and improve accuracy. Kmart acknowledges that 3D cannot yet replace all physical samples but can substitute many. Correlation between 3D and physical samples provides insights into fabric accuracy, handling improvements, and technical limitations, informing adjustments to asset libraries and handling standards. Setting realistic expectations for 3D samples helps avoid getting lost in technical issues and facilitates smoother adoption. --- ## Ambition of the 3D Journey: Technology-Focused or Holistic Transformation? This section discusses Kmart’s ambition to drive comprehensive digital transformation beyond technology adoption, addressing user skills, role evolution, and process integration. Kmart chose to "play the whole game," aiming for end-to-end digital transformation across multiple aspects and stakeholders, rather than focusing narrowly on technology implementation. Key focus areas include: - **3D User Skills:** Identifying desired skill sets for different scenarios, assessing current capabilities of in-house teams and suppliers, and implementing upskilling plans. - **Role Evolution:** Recognizing the emergence of new roles such as "3D merchandiser." Recruitment for such roles can be challenging, as industry awareness is still developing. - **3D Prototyping Process:** Establishing clear agendas and realistic roles for all participants to ensure engagement and clarity in the new workflow. - **System Integration:** Streamlining the development lifecycle through integration of digital systems to improve efficiency and communication. The team remains confident and excited about expanding their digital capabilities and achieving a broader transformation. --- ## Collaboration Strategy: Moving Forward Faster Alone or Further Together? This section highlights Kmart’s approach to collaboration across the industry ecosystem as a key enabler for sustainable progress. While decisions and rapid progress can be made within small groups, Kmart recognizes that relying solely on internal opinions risks limited perspectives and potential setbacks. They emphasize the importance of: - **Small Collaborations:** Working together with in-house teams, suppliers, software companies, and other industry partners. - **Openness and Resource Sharing:** Exchanging information and resources openly to receive input and feedback aligned with industry trends.

They emphasize the importance of: - **Small Collaborations:** Working together with in-house teams, suppliers, software companies, and other industry partners. - **Openness and Resource Sharing:** Exchanging information and resources openly to receive input and feedback aligned with industry trends. - **Joint Adaptation:** Adjusting directions collaboratively based on shared insights, recognizing the uncertainty of the future. Kmart sees forums and platforms for knowledge exchange as meaningful opportunities to foster this collaborative environment and create new possibilities in digital transformation. --- # Summary Kmart Australia’s 3D exploration journey exemplifies a strategic and ambitious approach to digital transformation in apparel development. By starting with complex products, committing to full digital workflows, investing in user skills and role evolution, and embracing industry collaboration, Kmart is positioning itself to lead the future of 3D prototyping and development in retail fashion.
